title: Natural Hazards & Human Activities

competencies.text: Describe human modification of landforms since Neolithic (~6,000 BCE).
Assess hazards (tropical cyclones, ipo-ipo, thunderstorms, storm surges, heat waves).

days.title: Humans Reshape the Land
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

This week you will describe how humans have modified landforms since the Neolithic period (about 6,000 BCE) and assess hazards such as tropical cyclones, ipo-ipo, thunderstorms, storm surges and heat waves.

🏺 From Farming to Megacities

PeriodActivitiesEffects on landforms
Neolithic (from about 6,000 BCE)Early farming, clearing forests, settlementsSmall clearings, early terraces, more erosion
Ancient civilizationsIrrigation canals, dams, citiesRivers redirected; floodplains changed
Industrial eraMining, railways, factoriesMountains cut, valleys filled
Modern eraHighways, mega-dams, reclamation, quarryingCoastlines moved; rivers channeled; land subsiding

🇵🇭 Philippine Examples

  • Ifugao rice terraces — a sustainable, centuries-old reshaping of mountains.
  • Manila Bay reclamation — new land built from the sea, changing currents and drainage.
  • Quarrying and mining in Rizal and elsewhere — cut hills, silted rivers.
  • Deforestation — loss of forest cover in many uplands.

Some changes reduce hazards (well-built drainage, terraces), while others increase them (cutting slopes, filling wetlands).

✅ Quick Check

3 questions — read each explanation.

scenario.text: What major change in human life began in the Neolithic period?

choices.label: People began farming and settling in villages
People first began using smartphones and cars
People started building large steel factories
People first learned to mine coal for trains

scenario.explanation: The Neolithic saw the start of agriculture and permanent settlements, which began to change landforms.

scenario.text: Which is an example of SUSTAINABLE landform modification in the Philippines?

choices.label: The Ifugao rice terraces
Illegal quarrying of hills
Filling in a mangrove swamp
Clear-cutting a watershed

scenario.explanation: The terraces reshape slopes while controlling water and erosion and have lasted for centuries.

scenario.text: Why can reclaiming land from the sea increase flood risk in nearby areas?

choices.label: It can block natural drainage and change water flow
It makes the nearby sea much colder and calmer
It removes all of the rain clouds from the coastal city
It lowers the sea level along the whole coast

scenario.explanation: Reclaimed land can alter currents and block river outlets and drainage, so water backs up into nearby communities.

days.title: Hazards and Disasters
days.content:
🧩 Key Terms

TermMeaning
HazardA natural or human-caused event that could cause harm
ExposurePeople and property located where the hazard can strike
VulnerabilityHow easily they are harmed (weak houses, poverty, no warning)
CapacityResources and skills to cope (drills, savings, strong buildings)
DisasterSerious disruption when a hazard hits an exposed, vulnerable community

⛈️ Local Weather Hazards

  • Thunderstorms — lightning, strong gusts, heavy rain that can cause flash floods. When thunder roars, go indoors.
  • Ipo-ipo (buhawi) — a small, intense rotating column of air from a strong thunderstorm; short-lived but can destroy light houses and crops along a narrow path.
  • Tropical cyclones and storm surges — large-scale, long-lasting threats.
  • Heat waves — extended high heat index; risk of heat stroke.

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each term to its meaning. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.why: It is not yet a disaster.

match.right: Hazard striking an exposed, vulnerable community
How easily people or property are harmed
Small, intense rotating column of air
Storm with lightning and heavy rain

match.why: Roots no longer hold the soil.
It works with OCD and LGUs.

days.title: Assessing Hazards
days.content:
📊 Assessing Risk

To assess a hazard in your community, ask:

  1. What hazards occur here, and how often? (Use PAGASA and PHIVOLCS data and hazard maps.)
  2. Who and what is exposed? (Homes near rivers, coasts or steep slopes.)
  3. How vulnerable are they? (Building materials, age, health, access to warnings.)
  4. What capacities exist? (Evacuation centers, drills, early warning systems.)

⬆️ Human Activities That Raise Risk

  • Building on floodplains, riverbanks, fault lines or steep slopes
  • Deforestation and quarrying
  • Clogging drains with garbage
  • Over-pumping groundwater (subsidence)
  • Removing mangroves

⬇️ Activities That Lower Risk

  • Reforestation and mangrove planting
  • Proper drainage and waste segregation
  • Following land-use plans and building codes
  • Early warning systems and drills

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Assess the hazards. Read every explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: A forested hillside in Rizal is cleared for a subdivision. A year later, heavy rain causes a landslide. What MOST increased the risk?

choices.label: Removing trees whose roots held the soil
Adding more trees to the steep hillside
Building drainage canals along the slope
Rain falling more slowly than in the past

scenario.explanation: Tree roots bind soil and absorb water. Without them, saturated slopes fail more easily.

scenario.text: An ipo-ipo forms over an open field during a thunderstorm. What should nearby residents do?

choices.label: Shelter in a sturdy building, away from windows
Go outside to record a video of it up close
Hide in a light nipa hut in the middle of the field
Stand under a tall tree until it passes by

scenario.explanation: Ipo-ipo winds can destroy light structures and throw debris. A sturdy building and an interior room are safest.

scenario.text: Two barangays face the same typhoon. One has strong houses and an early warning system; the other does not. Which statement is TRUE?

choices.label: The second barangay has higher disaster risk
Both barangays have exactly the same level of risk
The first barangay has higher disaster risk
Risk depends only on the typhoon's strength

scenario.explanation: Risk depends on hazard, exposure and vulnerability. Lower vulnerability and higher capacity reduce risk.

scenario.text: During El Niño, the heat index in your town reaches 43 °C. What is the MAIN health risk?

choices.label: Heat exhaustion and heat stroke
Hypothermia from cold winds
Frostbite on fingers and toes
Snow blindness from bright light

scenario.explanation: A heat index above 42 °C is in the Danger range, where heat cramps and exhaustion are likely and heat stroke is possible.

scenario.text: A barangay wants to reduce flood risk. Which combination is BEST?

choices.label: Clear drains, segregate waste, reforest uplands
Pave all open soil and fill in all the creeks and streams
Build houses closer to the riverbanks
Burn garbage that clogs the canals

scenario.explanation: Clean drains and proper waste disposal let water flow; upland forests slow runoff — together they lower flood risk.

days.title: Living Wisely With Hazards
days.content:
🗺️ Land-Use Planning

LGUs prepare a Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP) that uses hazard maps to decide where homes, schools and industries should — and should not — be built. No-build zones along rivers, coasts and fault lines save lives over the long term.

🌳 Nature-Based Solutions

Healthy ecosystems are natural defenses: mangroves reduce storm-surge waves, forests hold soil and slow floods, wetlands store floodwater, and coral reefs break waves before they reach the shore. Protecting them is cheaper than rebuilding after disasters.

🧠 Big Idea

Humans have changed landforms for 8,000 years. Today we can choose changes that reduce hazards instead of increasing them — and every household can help by keeping drains clear, planting trees and following warnings.

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

3 lives, 6 keys. You need 70% (5 of 6). Read each explanation.

escape.text: What is the difference between a hazard and a disaster?

choices.label: A disaster is a hazard's serious impact
A hazard is always bigger than a disaster
They mean exactly the same thing in DRRM
A disaster happens only at sea, and never on land

escape.explanation: A hazard becomes a disaster when it hits an exposed, vulnerable community and causes serious losses.

choices.label: A small, intense rotating column of air
A large ocean wave from an undersea earthquake
A volcanic mudflow down a river
A long period with no rainfall

escape.explanation: Ipo-ipo (buhawi) is a tornado-like whirlwind formed from strong thunderstorms.

escape.text: Which human activity MOST increases flood risk in cities?

choices.label: Garbage clogging drains and canals
Planting more trees along the city streets
Building rain gardens in parks
Restoring wetlands near rivers

escape.explanation: Clogged drains stop water from flowing away, so even moderate rain floods streets.

escape.text: Which natural ecosystem BEST reduces storm-surge damage on coasts?

choices.label: Mangrove forests
Rice paddy fields
Grasslands
Pine forests in the highlands

escape.explanation: Mangroves' dense roots and trunks slow waves and trap sediment along the shore.

escape.text: Which agency coordinates national disaster response in the Philippines?

choices.label: NDRRMC
PAGASA
DepEd
PHIVOLCS

escape.explanation: The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council coordinates disaster response with the Office of Civil Defense.

escape.text: What does a Comprehensive Land Use Plan use hazard maps for?

choices.label: Deciding where it is safe to build
Choosing the colors of school uniforms
Setting the prices of rice in markets
Planning the routes of jeepneys only

escape.explanation: Hazard maps guide where homes and facilities should or should not be built.
